magnitude: Small income elasticities with respect to car ownership when accounting for panel nature; no numeric value given in abstract
method: dynamic logit with unobserved heterogeneity (Wooldridge estimator) on household panel
verification_note: Abstract reports small positive income elasticities of car ownership from dynamic panel logit models, without explicit causal language, and household car ownership (not cars per 1,000) is the measured outcome.

title: Longitudinal Analysis of Car Ownership and car Travel Demand in the Paris Region using a Pseudo-panel Data Approach
magnitude: Income elasticity of car ownership of 0.47; influence decreasing with rising income and not significant for high-income households; not a determinant in the most urbanized area but positive in car-dependent areas
method: pseudo-panel (cohorts built from repeated cross-sections) with semi-log linear regression specification
verification_note: Pseudo-panel cohort analysis estimates income elasticity of 0.47 on car ownership (cars per household, close proxy to cars per 1,000), a positive association not framed as strictly causal.

title: Income's effect on car and vehicle ownership, worldwide: 1960–2015
venue: Transportation Research Part A Policy and Practice
magnitude: Income elasticity of car ownership about 2.0 for low- and middle-income levels, falling to zero as ownership saturates at the highest income levels
lag: short-run and long-run elasticities estimated (dynamic specification)
geography: 26 countries including OECD countries (incl. European), China, India, Pakistan
method: dynamically specified econometric model (short- and long-run income elasticities) estimated on annual country data, 1960–1992
verification_note: Panel of 26 countries over 1960-1992 is used to econometrically estimate dynamic models of car ownership as a function of per-capita income, a positive causal elasticity relationship, though car/population ratio is a close but not identical proxy for 'cars per 1,000'.

title: A dynamic random effects multinomial logit model of household car ownership
venue: Research at the University of Copenhagen (University of Copenhagen)
magnitude: "Relatively small elasticities with respect to income and car costs are estimated" (no numeric value given in abstract)
method: dynamic random effects multinomial logit with correlated random effects
verification_note: The abstract reports small income elasticities of household car ownership from a dynamic panel multinomial model, not a direct causal estimate of cars per 1,000 population.

title: A CROSS-COUNTRY COMPARISON OF HOUSEHOLD, CAR OWNERSHIP
geography: France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, Poland, UK, USA (Italian macro-regions North/Centre vs South/Islands)
method: Age-Cohort-Period model; long-term projections
verification_note: The Age-Cohort-Period model uses panel data and shows income positively associated with car ownership rates (sensitivity to income/economic factors), though framed as association/projection rather than strict causal identification.

title: Comparing urban form influences on travel distance, car ownership, and mode choice
venue: Transportation Research Part D Transport and Environment
magnitude: Exponential reduction of car use with higher population density, clearly demonstrated with aggregate city data; nonlinear relationships; urban form thresholds identified. No numeric coefficient or elasticity reported in abstract.
method: gradient boosting decision tree and regression models on disaggregated data across 19 cities
verification_note: Abstract reports exponential reduction of car use (not exactly 'cars per 1,000' but closely related car ownership/mode choice measure) with higher population density using gradient boosting/regression on cross-sectional city data, without explicit causal language.

title: Impact analysis of population density on car ownership, type chioce and usage
venue: Journal of the City Planning Institute of Japan
magnitude: Elasticities computed for car ownership and usage models where density is significant; single-person households show larger elasticities than non-single households; usage model elasticity larger than ownership model. Numeric values not given in abstract.
method: household-level micro data regression (car ownership, vehicle type, and usage models by household type), with green party vote share as a bias-control variable
verification_note: Abstract reports population density affects car ownership and usage (typically negatively, as is standard in such models) using cross-sectional household survey data without causal framing, and car ownership is a close proxy for cars per 1,000.

title: The Spatio-temporal Variations of Urban Private Car Ownership in China and Their Influencing Factors
magnitude: Increases of urban population density can inhibit the rapid increase of private car ownership (no coefficient or elasticity reported in abstract)
method: panel data model (10 explanatory variables) across 235 Chinese cities, 1990-2009
verification_note: Abstract states urban population density increases inhibit the rapid increase of private car ownership, based on a panel data model across 235 Chinese cities.

title: Cars, Community, and the Urban Landscape: Exploring the Spatial Patterns of Car Ownership and Associated Factors Using Geographically Weighted Regression
venue: International Journal of Architectural Engineering and Urban Research
method: OLS and geographically weighted regression (GWR) on 2017 NHTS data, with Global Moran's I and Getis-Ord general G for spatial autocorrelation
verification_note: Study uses OLS/GWR cross-sectional regression on NHTS survey data to show population density is negatively associated with car ownership, not a causal design.

title: Traffic fatalities and economic growth
magnitude: No elasticity or coefficient reported in abstract
method: econometric models of fatality rate (F/P), motorization (V/P), and fatalities per vehicle (F/V) against per capita income; decomposition F/P = V/P x F/V
verification_note: The paper models vehicles-per-person (motorization) as one component affecting fatalities-per-person across 88 countries 1963-99, finding growth in V/P raises fatalities in developing countries but is outweighed by falling F/V in industrialized ones, implying a mixed net relationship without a strict causal design.

title: Analysis of the Impact of Road Infrastructure and Economic and Transport Factors on Road Safety in Poland
magnitude: Log-linear regression elasticities estimated; the abstract states greater motorization increases accident risk but reports no numeric elasticity value for motorization.
method: log-linear regression on time-series of national data, 2010–2024
verification_note: The study uses log-linear regression on 2010–2024 Polish time-series/panel data showing motorization (cars per 1,000) is associated with increased accidents (proxy for road deaths), described as elasticity associations rather than a causal identification strategy.

title: The effect of public transport quality on car ownership – A source of wider benefits?
method: estimated model using county panel data, 1986-2015
verification_note: Panel data from 21 Swedish counties 1986-2015 is used to estimate that better public transport service (of which rail density is a component) reduces car ownership, implying a negative effect of rail density on cars per 1,000.

title: Hysteresis & Urban Rail
venue: European journal of transport and infrastructure research
magnitude: Current density and travel behaviour are measurably influenced by past access to rail; no coefficient or elasticity reported in abstract
method: tract-level regression of current density and auto ownership/travel behaviour on historical (1865, 1925) rail access, with robustness checks across causal, functional, and spatial specifications
verification_note: Abstract claims past rail access lowers auto ownership (higher density, lower auto ownership desirable outcome of rail reuse), but no explicit coefficient on 'rail density' vs 'cars per 1,000' is reported, and rail is proxied by historical access rather than a density measure.

title: Exploring the Effect of Bicycle Infrastructure on Car Usage: A Case Study in Huhhot, China
magnitude: A 100 m reduction in walking distance to bicycle stations has the same effect on driving probability as an increase in parking fees of about 2.00 yuan/h (US$0.30/h); providing bike lanes is equivalent to about 3.00 yuan/h (US$0.45/h) in parking fees.
method: mixed logit model with random coefficients on stated preference survey data; equivalence analysis converting bicycle infrastructure changes into equivalent parking fee changes
verification_note: The stated preference survey/mixed logit model estimates how bike infrastructure (lanes, station proximity) reduces car use probability, not a direct measure of 'cycling network density' causing 'cars per 1,000'.

title: Sustainable Economic Development and Greenhouse Gas Emissions: The Dynamic Impact of Renewable Energy Consumption, GDP, and Corruption
magnitude: A 1% increase in renewable energy is associated with a decline in GHG in the interval (0.166103, 0.220551)
lag: 2000–2016 panel; no explicit lag structure stated in abstract
method: dynamic panel model (EKC framework with GDP, corruption controls); estimator not specified in abstract
verification_note: Panel data regression shows increasing renewable energy share by 1% leads to a decline in GHG emissions, treated by authors as a causal relationship, though GHG measure is total/aggregate rather than strictly per capita.

title: Domestic material consumption and greenhouse gas emissions in the EU ‐28 countries: Implications for environmental sustainability targets
magnitude: Abstract reports that renewable energy development improves environmental sustainability in both short and long run; no coefficient or elasticity given in abstract
lag: short run and long run (no specific horizons stated)
method: panel econometric analysis (short- and long-run estimates; estimator not specified in abstract)
verification_note: Abstract states renewable energy share improves (reduces) environmental degradation/GHG emissions in both short and long run, based on panel estimation for EU-28, though GHG per capita is proxied by broader environmental sustainability/quality measure.

title: Climate-related development finance and renewable energy consumption in greenhouse gas emissions reduction in the Congo basin
magnitude: Abstract reports that an increase in renewable energy consumption reduces GHG emissions; no coefficient or elasticity given in abstract
method: panel regression (estimator not specified in abstract)
verification_note: Abstract states renewable energy consumption reduces GHG emissions using panel regression, though renewables share (vs consumption level) and GHG per capita (vs total GHG) are close proxies rather than exact matches.

title: Renewable energy and CO2 emissions: New evidence with the panel threshold model
magnitude: Growth in renewable energy consumption per capita has a negative and significant effect on growth of CO2 emissions per capita only when countries surpass a certain threshold of renewable energy consumption; no effect reported below the threshold. No numeric coefficient given in abstract.
method: dynamic panel threshold model robust to cross-section dependence
verification_note: Dynamic panel threshold model finds renewable energy consumption growth reduces CO2 emissions per capita growth only above a threshold, implying a conditional/mixed effect depending on level.

title: Decomposition Analysis in Electricity Sector Output from Carbon Emissions in China
magnitude: Electric output effect "played the most significant role in increasing CO2 emissions" from China's electric sector; no numeric elasticity given in abstract
method: multilevel Logarithmic Mean Divisia Index (LMDI) decomposition with decoupling index and electricity elasticity of emissions
verification_note: The study uses LMDI decomposition on China's electricity sector total CO2 emissions and output (not GHG per capita), finding electric output effect increases emissions, which is a decomposition/accounting association rather than a causal estimate of demand on per-capita GHG.

title: Temperature and Residential Electricity Demand for Heating and Cooling in G7 Economies: A Method of Moments Panel Quantile Regression Approach
magnitude: Not quantified in the abstract; described only as statistically and positively responsive to cold days rather than hot days
geography: G7 economies (includes Germany, France, Italy, UK, plus US, Canada, Japan)
method: panel fixed effects with Driscoll-Kraay SEs, second-generation panel unit root/cointegration, and method of moments panel quantile regression (MM-QR)
verification_note: Abstract reports residential electricity demand is statistically and positively responsive to cold days (heating-related) using panel fixed effects/MM-QR, an associational elasticity estimate rather than a strict causal design.

title: Regional heterogeneous drivers of electricity demand in Saudi Arabia: Modeling regional residential electricity demand
magnitude: Abstract states only that hot weather conditions "significantly impact" residential electricity demand in all regions; no elasticity or coefficient for weather/cooling variable is reported in the abstract.
geography: Saudi Arabia (Central, Eastern, Western, Southern regions)
method: Structural Time Series Modeling (regional residential electricity demand)
verification_note: Abstract reports hot weather conditions significantly impact residential electricity demand via structural time series modeling across regions, implying a positive effect but without explicit causal identification or exact cooling degree days coefficient.

title: Climate, Extreme Heat, and Electricity Demand in California
venue: Journal of Applied Meteorology and Climatology
magnitude: Projected extreme-heat days increase ~2x (inland cities, e.g., Sacramento, Fresno) to ~4x (coastal cities, e.g., Los Angeles, San Diego) present-day numbers by 2070–99; mapped onto observed high-temperature–electricity demand relationships, potential electricity deficits up to 17% during T90 peak demand periods
method: climate projections from three AOGCMs (SRES A1fi, B1, and a middle scenario) combined with observed temperature–electricity demand relationships for California
verification_note: The abstract discusses extreme heat/temperature projections mapped onto observed high-temperature–electricity demand relationships, not cooling degree days specifically, and claims are projection-based associations rather than a formally identified causal effect.

title: Effects of climate change on heating and cooling degree days and potential energy demand in the household sector of China
magnitude: Population-weighted CDD increases are outweighed by larger HDD decreases, giving an overall decrease of about 15% in potential energy demand; increases in cooling demand in the south and parts of northern China; reference-temperature changes yield ~80% increase in energy demand
lag: 21st century projections (multiple future periods and scenarios)
method: regional climate model projections of HDD/CDD weighted by population projections
verification_note: CDD increases are projected to increase cooling energy demand (though overall energy demand falls due to larger HDD decreases), based on climate model simulations rather than a designed causal identification strategy.

title: Modeling and predicting provincial per capita electricity consumption in Türkiye: A panel data and machine learning approach
magnitude: Cooling degree days reported as positively associated with per capita electricity consumption; no coefficient or elasticity given in abstract
lag: 2015–2023 annual panel; no lag structure stated
method: Two-way fixed-effects panel estimation, complemented by Random Forest machine learning
verification_note: Abstract reports CDD positively associated with per capita electricity consumption via two-way fixed-effects panel estimation, framed as association not causal.

title: Economic valuation of climate change–induced mortality: age dependent cold and heat mortality in the Netherlands
magnitude: Sensitivity of mortality to temperature is 4.6%/°C on hot days and 2.1%/°C on cold days for the ≥80 years group; climate change first decreases total net mortality (dominated by fewer cold-related deaths), reversing under high warming scenarios; net economic costs up to €17.6 billion in 2085 under high warming
lag: Long time lags for extreme temperature effects on mortality, especially in cold; projections to 2050 and 2085
method: Projection model of temperature-mortality relationships by age class with demographic change, time lags and urban heat island effect; economic valuation (VSL, VSLY)
verification_note: The study models heat days' effect on mortality rates (not life expectancy directly), finding more heat days increase heat-related mortality, which would tend to reduce life expectancy.

title: Regional distribution of photovoltaic deployment in the UK and its determinants: A spatial econometric approach
method: spatial Durbin model (cross-sectional spatial econometrics) following traditional regression and general-to-specific selection
verification_note: Abstract states population density affects PV uptake via spatial regression but does not specify the direction of effect, and PV uptake is a proxy for renewables share rather than the exact quantity.

title: Renewable Energy in Final Energy Consumption and Income in the EU-28 Countries
magnitude: low and positive relationship between GDP per capita and share of RES in final consumption; no coefficient or elasticity reported in abstract
method: panel data models with causality testing (abstract does not specify estimator)
verification_note: Abstract reports a low but positive and significant causal relationship from real GDP per capita to the share of RES in final energy consumption using panel data models for EU-28 2007-2017.

title: Analyzing the Role of Renewables in Energy Security by Deploying Renewable Energy Security Index
venue: Journal of Sustainable Development of Energy Water and Environment Systems
magnitude: Research and Development "plays a critical role" in improving Norway's renewable energy security index; no coefficient or elasticity reported in abstract
method: Principal Component Analysis-based Renewable Energy Security Index with time-series analysis (method details not specified in abstract)
verification_note: R&D is reported as playing a critical role in improving the composite Renewable Energy Security Index (not directly the renewables share) using PCA-based index construction with likely time-series analysis.

title: The Role of Regional Determinants in the Deployment of Renewable Energy in Farms. The Case of Spain
magnitude: Regional R&D investment is reported as important/significant for farmers' decisions to invest in renewable energy generation; no coefficient or elasticity given in abstract
method: multilevel logit model on panel data
verification_note: The study uses a multilevel logit model on panel data to find regional R&D investment is a significant determinant of farmers' decisions to invest in renewable energy capacity, not a strict fixed-effects/GMM panel causal design.

title: The Role of Renewable Energy Policy and R&D in Renewables Diffusion
magnitude: Scenario analysis: higher R&D investment combined with strong policy support is associated with faster renewable growth; strong renewable energy policies could boost adoption by 100% to 200%. No elasticity reported for R&D alone.
method: scenario analysis (four scenarios varying R&D funding and policy support) up to 2040
verification_note: The paper uses scenario-based simulation to show higher R&D investment combined with policy support leads to faster renewable energy diffusion, though R&D's isolated effect is not separately quantified.

title: Population dependency ratios and economic growth in SAARC nations: Insights on aging and youth dynamics
venue: Journal of Infrastructure Policy and Development
method: Pooled Mean Group / ARDL (PMG/ARDL) panel estimation
verification_note: The study uses panel PMG/ARDL to show old-age dependency ratio positively affects economic growth, which is a proxy for GDP per inhabitant.

title: Impact of Dependency Ratio on Economic Growth: Evidence from Selected Asian Countries
geography: South Asia (Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Bhutan) and East Asia (Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Macau), 1971-2022
method: FMOLS (fully modified OLS) on unbalanced panel
verification_note: The abstract uses FMOLS panel data methods to show old dependency ratio has an adverse (negative) effect on GDP per capita growth, treating GDP per capita as a close proxy for GDP per inhabitant.

title: Effects of Demographic Change on Economic Growth: A Panel ARDL Approach for Selected OECD Countries
magnitude: Old-age dependency ratio has a negative effect on GDP per capita growth rate (no coefficient reported in abstract)
method: panel ARDL estimation
verification_note: Panel ARDL analysis of OECD countries finds old-age dependency ratio negatively affects GDP per capita growth rate, framed causally.

title: Population Aging and Economic Growth: The Chinese Experience of Solow Model
venue: International Journal of Economics and Finance
magnitude: Abstract states that in the long run population aging (old-age dependency ratio) has a positive effect on per-capita income growth, and the effect of aging exceeds that of the national savings rate; no numeric coefficient or elasticity reported in abstract
method: Solow-model steady-state derivation plus cointegration test on China 1978-2012
verification_note: Cointegration analysis of China 1978-2012 finds old-age dependency ratio positively affects GDP per-capita in the long run, though GDP per-capita is a close proxy for GDP per inhabitant.

title: The mediating role of human capital in the impact of demographic structure on economic growth: Evidence from Chinese provinces
magnitude: A 1% increase in the old-age dependency ratio is associated with an approximately 0.55% decline in real per capita GRP; a 1% increase in the child dependency ratio with a 0.29% decline. Health human capital (health workers per 1,000 population) mediates 14.3% of the old-age dependency total effect and 48.6% of the child dependency total effect; educational human capital mediation is not statistically significant.
lag: 2010–2024 panel; robustness with lagged dependency ratios
method: two-way fixed effects with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors; Baron-Kenny three-step mediation analysis on augmented Solow per capita GRP equation
verification_note: GDP per inhabitant is proxied by real per capita GRP (gross regional product) of Chinese provinces, and the old-age dependency ratio has a significant negative total effect on it via a two-way fixed effects panel model with mediation analysis.

title: Population aging and economic growth: evidence from ASEAN countries
magnitude: Old-age dependency is reported to harm GDP per capita growth; no numeric coefficient or elasticity given in the abstract
method: fixed effect model (FEM)
verification_note: The abstract explicitly states old-age dependency harms GDP per capita growth using a fixed effects panel model on ASEAN countries, treating it as a causal impact.

title: Investigating the effect of Dynamics Employment and Institutional factors with a focus on Economic Freedom and Ease Doing of Business on GDP per capita in Iran
venue: International Journal of Innovation in Management Economics and Social Sciences
method: generalized time series torque method (as stated in abstract; likely GMM-type estimator, not further specified)
verification_note: Abstract reports employment rate has a positive impact on GDP per capita using a generalized time-series method, framed as a causal effect.

title: Impact of Educational Attainment on Employment Outcomes in Jammu and Kashmir
venue: International Journal of Advanced Engineering and Management Research
magnitude: Higher educational attainment is associated with lower inactivity rates but higher unemployment; no straightforward improvement in employment outcomes. No coefficient or effect size reported in abstract.
method: descriptive analysis of PLFS data (employment status and occupation/industry breakdowns by education level)
verification_note: Higher education correlates with lower inactivity but higher unemployment, indicating no straightforward positive effect on employment rate, based on descriptive PLFS data analysis without causal identification.

title: Assessing the effect of income inequality on household energy poverty—empirical evidence from China
magnitude: Abstract states the increase in household income raises affordability and can lift households out of energy poverty; no coefficient or elasticity reported in the abstract
method: fixed panel modeling (with energy income response modeling and income inequality measurement) on Chinese household data for 2016, 2018, 2020
verification_note: Household income increase raises affordability and reduces energy poverty risk, per fixed-panel model analysis in the abstract.

title: Impact of Households’ Income Sources on Child’s Multidimensional Poverty in South Africa
venue: Journal of Epidemiology and Global Health
magnitude: Income sources (social grants, salaries, business income, remittances, pensions, other) associated with significantly lower (p<0.01) fuzzy child MPI vs control; once-off grants associated with significantly higher fuzzy MPI (p<0.01). No coefficient magnitudes reported in abstract.
method: Tobit regression with treatment effects potential outcome framework (ATE/ATET via regression adjustment) on fuzzy child MPI
verification_note: The study uses Tobit regression and treatment-effects/regression-adjustment estimators on cross-sectional survey data on income sources (not overall household income) and finds mixed effects on fuzzy multidimensional poverty, not a quasi-experimental design.

title: Impact of Gini Ratio, Economic Growth and Unemployment on Poverty Levels: A Panel Data Analysis
venue: International Journal of Economics and Financial Issues
magnitude: Gini ratio has a significant partial effect on poverty rate; no coefficient or elasticity reported in abstract
method: panel data regression (fixed/random effects not specified in abstract)
verification_note: Abstract reports Gini ratio significantly affects poverty rate via panel data regression but does not state direction explicitly nor claim strict causality beyond statistical significance.

title: Working life gain from gain in old age life expectancy in India
method: not stated in abstract
verification_note: Abstract only poses the research question about longevity, work participation, and old age dependency without reporting findings or a causal effect.

title: Aging of rural population in Yugoslavia
geography: Yugoslavia (FR of Yugoslavia) and its republics and provinces, rural and urban populations, 1961-1991
method: descriptive analysis of census age indicators (share of age groups, average age, ageing index) over 1961-1991 censuses
verification_note: The abstract attributes rural population aging (reflected in average age/median age indicators) to out-migration of young people from rural areas, based on descriptive census comparisons rather than a controlled design.

title: The Impact of Migration on Age Structure Conducive to Human Development Across the Urban Hierarchy
magnitude: Migration generally increases the working-age share in cities (strongest in big cities) but reduces it in rural areas; effect weakens and reverses in smaller towns and rural areas. No numeric coefficient reported in abstract.
geography: 46 developing countries (Global South), subnational urban hierarchy
method: analysis of 103 microcensuses from 46 developing countries (regression on working-age share by urban hierarchy level)
verification_note: Abstract reports migration's effect on working-age population share (not median age directly), with positive effect in cities and negative in rural areas, using microcensus cross-sectional data.

title: Relationship between Rural Built Environment and Household Vehicle Ownership: An Empirical Analysis in Rural Sichuan, China
magnitude: Abstract reports no coefficient or elasticity; states that with increases in road density (among building density and destination accessibility), an increase in high-carbon vehicle ownership is an inevitable trend among rural households
geography: seven typical villages in rural Sichuan, China
method: multinomial logit (MNL) model on household survey data with GIS-measured built environment variables
verification_note: Cross-sectional MNL survey data show road density positively associated with high-carbon vehicle ownership, not a causal experimental design, and vehicle ownership category is a close proxy for cars per 1,000.

title: Projection of passenger cars’ fuel demand and greenhouse gas emissions in Iran by 2050
magnitude: PC stock triples to 64 million by 2050, resulting in a 280% increase in gasoline demand and GHG emissions under business-as-usual scenario
method: econometric projection models of PC stock and use intensity, with survival-rate function and back-calculation, feeding a fuel demand and GHG emissions projection
verification_note: The study projects PC stock growth and GHG emissions together via econometric/survival models (not per-capita GHG, and no explicit cars-per-1000 causal link isolated), reflecting an associative projection rather than a tested causal effect.

title: Typology of US metropolitan areas illuminates per-capita mobile greenhouse gas emissions impacts and informs mitigation strategies
magnitude: Abstract reports no numeric coefficient or elasticity; states only that car use exacerbates per-capita mobile emissions (PMGEs), with the sign inferred from the qualitative SHAP-based finding.
method: factor analysis, Gaussian mixture clustering, extreme gradient boosting regression with SHAP values
verification_note: Machine learning (XGBoost+SHAP) predictive model shows car use is associated with higher PMGEs, but this is a cross-sectional predictive/explanatory analysis, not a causal design, and 'car use' is a broader proxy than the specific 'cars per 1,000' metric.

title: Electricity Consumption, Carbon Emissions and Economic Growth in Nigeria
venue: International Journal of Energy Economics and Policy
method: Multivariate VECM with Granger causality tests
verification_note: VECM/Granger analysis finds electricity consumption increases carbon emissions in Nigeria, but emissions (total) rather than GHG per capita is measured.

title: Residual electricity demand: An empirical investigation
magnitude: Heating and cooling degree influences residual demand much more than they influence total demand (no coefficient reported in abstract)
geography: a single country (national-level temperature and demand; country not named in abstract)
method: linear and quantile regression models
verification_note: Abstract reports heating/cooling degree influence demand without specifying direction of effect, uses regression models without causal identification strategy, and electricity demand is a close proxy for the broader concept rather than exact match to residual demand focus.

title: Residential Electricity Demand in Arkansas
venue: DigitalCommons@UTEP (The University of Texas at El Paso)
method: residential electricity demand model with heating degree days as explanatory variable (estimator not stated in abstract)
verification_note: Abstract describes a regression demand model with heating degree days as an explanatory variable but does not report the sign or magnitude of its effect on electricity demand.

title: Residential Electricity Consumption in Las Cruces, New Mexico, USA
magnitude: Long-run: residential consumption does not respond in a statistically reliable manner to any explanatory variable (including heating degree days). Short-run: consumption responds reliably to variations in heating/degree days (direction and size not stated in abstract).
lag: Long-run and short-run (short-run responses reported; exact lag lengths not stated)
method: Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) model with long-run and short-run elasticities
verification_note: ARDL long-run/short-run elasticities show statistically insignificant long-run response but reliable short-run response to heating degree days, with sign expected but not explicitly stated as positive or negative in the abstract.

title: Climatic impacts on electricity consumption of urban residential buildings in China
magnitude: A 1% increase in HDD is linked to a 0.457% rise in electricity consumption per unit of floor space in urban residential buildings
method: county-level unbalanced panel regression
verification_note: The study uses a county-level panel dataset to estimate the causal effect of HDD on electricity consumption per unit floor space, finding a positive elasticity, though electricity consumption per floor space is a proxy for overall electricity demand.

title: Projection of residential and commercial electricity consumption under SSPs in Jiangsu province, China
magnitude: CDD coefficient is about 3 times the HDD coefficient; no HDD coefficient value stated in the abstract
method: linear regression model (climate and socioeconomic factors) plus policy model, projected under SSPs
verification_note: The linear/policy models regress electricity consumption on HDD (and CDD) as climate factors with a positive coefficient, but this is a statistical projection model rather than a causal identification strategy.

title: The increasing impact of weather on electricity supply and demand
magnitude: Peak demand rising above 70 GW due to electric heating (weather-driven demand variability; no explicit heating degree day coefficient reported)
method: Renewables.ninja and DESSTINEE model simulation of hourly electricity supply and demand under National Grid Two Degrees scenario
verification_note: The abstract models weather-driven electric heating demand and peak demand increases but does not explicitly quantify heating degree days as a variable, only describing simulated impacts of weather on electricity demand.

title: Effects of Extreme Temperatures on Years of Life Lost for Cardiovascular Deaths: A Time Series Study in Brisbane, Australia
magnitude: U-shaped exposure-response between daily mean temperature and years of life lost (CVD); lowest YLL at 24°C; sharper rise at heat extremes than cold; heat effect greatest on day of exposure; significant added effects of heat waves. No single coefficient reported in abstract.
lag: Heat effect greatest on day of exposure (lag 0); cold effect peaks 2 days after exposure
method: distributed lag nonlinear model (time series regression with trend, season, day-of-week, humidity adjustment)
verification_note: The study examines heat/cold effects on years of life lost (YLL) due to CVD, not life expectancy directly, and more heat days would increase YLL (a proxy inversely related to life expectancy), with associations rather than causal claims made.

title: The Impact of Climate Change on Life Expectancy in the UK: Empirical Evidence from Fourier Bootstrap ARDL Procedure
magnitude: Surface temperature change significantly reduces life expectancy in the long run; no significant short-run relationship. Coefficient not stated in abstract.
method: Fourier bootstrap ARDL cointegration with Toda-Yamamoto causality test; government expenditure as control
verification_note: The abstract uses surface temperature change (not specifically heat days count) as proxy for climate change, finding it reduces life expectancy long-run with causality evidence from Toda-Yamamoto test.

title: Urban density and residential solar adoption: evidence and theory
magnitude: Inverted U-shaped relationship between urban population density and residential PV installation; no coefficient or elasticity stated in abstract
method: Empirical evidence (method not specified in abstract) plus theoretical urban model incorporating residential PV adoption
verification_note: The study finds an inverted U-shaped (non-monotonic) relationship between population density and residential PV installation, not renewables share generally, combining empirical evidence with an explanatory urban model.

title: Renewable Energy in the Electricity Sector and GDP per Capita in the European Union
magnitude: positive but very low impact of GDP per capita on RES share in electricity (no coefficient given in abstract); causality not identified
geography: European Union member states (Luxembourg excluded as outlier)
method: panel data models (estimator not specified in abstract); cluster analysis as supplementary
verification_note: Panel data models show a positive but very low impact of GDP per capita on RES electricity share, but the authors explicitly state causality was not identified.

title: On the Impact of GDP per Capita, Carbon Intensity and Innovation for Renewable Energy Consumption: Worldwide Evidence
magnitude: GDP per capita promotes renewable energy consumption when it surpasses the 5000 USD threshold; no coefficient or elasticity reported in the abstract
geography: 94 countries worldwide, plus five income-based subpanels
method: heterogeneous panel fixed-effects (static and dynamic) with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors
verification_note: Abstract reports GDP per capita promotes renewable energy consumption (REC) above a threshold using fixed-effects panel estimation, and REC is a close proxy for renewables share rather than an exact match.
